top_stories.title: Claude/Anthropic Researcher Claims Proof of the Riemann Hypothesis
points: Anthropic mathematician Levent Alpöge used Claude to produce a proof of the Riemann Hypothesis (a 167-year-old unsolved problem from 1859 asking whether prime numbers follow a predictable pattern) after about 6 weeks of work.

The proof spans 17 million lines of machine-verifiable code and was certified correct by the Lean proof checker (automated software that verifies mathematical proofs line-by-line) and the Mathlib community.
The Riemann Hypothesis carries a $1 million Millennium Prize from the Clay Institute, established in 2000.

Alpöge said Claude 'far outpaced' him in the final stretch of the work, and critics (including the Association for Human Mathematics) called the proof 'little more than publicity,' arguing no human can reasonably verify 17 million lines of code.

A rival proof from Alessandro Masullo, reportedly produced without AI over 12 years, surfaced hours later but reviewers quickly flagged errors in it; top mathematicians had expected this problem to take decades more to solve.

unique_angles.point: Alpöge suggested more AI-driven mathematical 'miracles' are ahead, feeding into broader superintelligence timeline claims from industry figures like Meta's AI chief.

top_stories.title: OpenAI's Proposed Shared AI Capability Limits via Perplexity Metric
points: OpenAI chief scientist Jakub Pachocki proposed that frontier AI labs agree on shared capability thresholds measured by perplexity/log-perplexity (a measure of how well a model predicts the next word in text; lower scores mean better predictions), and published OpenAI's own numbers: GPT-3.5 at 0.99, GPT-4 at 0.91.
Scores below 0.8 correlate with emerging transformative abilities in cybersecurity and mathematics; around 0.76 is when OpenAI's models began producing results on open math problems.
An unreleased internal OpenAI model reportedly sits at about 0.73, with Pachocki predicting 'transformative capabilities' in the 0.68–0.7 range.
Sam Altman called the post 'the most important thing OpenAI has published in a while' and recommended rival labs agree on shared limits until AI monitoring tools catch up with capabilities.

The metric has notable gaps: different labs use different datasets making cross-lab comparisons difficult, perplexity doesn't map cleanly to specific real-world tasks, and chain-of-thought reasoning improvements (letting a model show step-by-step reasoning) don't necessarily lower perplexity scores.

unique_angles.point: Success of the proposal depends on whether other labs publish their own perplexity numbers and on concrete 'understanding' milestones, such as successor tools to chain-of-thought monitors that catch problems in model reasoning.

items.title: Coding Agents Struggle with Real-World Task Completion
points: SWE-CoWork tested 11 models on 101 workplace-style assignments with conflicting requirements scattered across simulated colleagues; top models passed only 63% of key fail-to-pass tests but completed fewer than 8% of full assignments.
31% of requirements agents reported as finished actually failed verification tests, exposing a gap between partially correct work and fully completed tasks.

Giving models all requirements upfront improved test scores by about 16 points for two models but did not improve full task completion, pointing to requirement tracking and verification as the core problem rather than initial clarity.
Proposed fixes include having agents list requirements before coding, flag ambiguous items, verify each requirement post-change, and explicitly name anything left unfinished.

items.title: AI Transparency Backlash in Gaming
points: Nicalis removed AI-generated music from The Binding of Isaac after players discovered Suno metadata (hidden file labels revealing the AI tool used to generate the audio) embedded in the tracks.
The incident shows that audio and other files retain evidence of their AI origins, and that disclosing AI use upfront is far easier than managing backlash after fans find proof.
Developers shipping creative work should assume fans will check file metadata and that admitting undisclosed AI use becomes much harder once controversy erupts.

items.title: Major AI Deals and Security Warnings
points: Palo Alto Networks agreed to acquire Applied Compute for $4.5 billion to help enterprises customize and deploy open-weight AI models, with closing expected in fiscal Q3 2027.
Amazon was reportedly nearing a $7.5 billion purchase of AI video startup Decart, potentially closing within a week.

OpenRouter removed three inference providers and stripped 125 endpoints of Zero Data Retention eligibility after researchers found the providers weren't upholding data-handling policies; OpenRouter's own systems were not breached.
More than 50 AI and security leaders expect increasingly sophisticated and disruptive cyberattacks within the next 18 months.

items.title: Real-World AI Workflows from Staff
points: Head of Sales uses Granola to record discovery calls, then has Claude extract the buyer's own stated needs to draft proposals from those words rather than templates, enabling roughly 10-minute turnaround while buyer engagement is high.

An editor uses Claude with MCP connectors (Machine-readable Code Protocol, a way for AI tools to fetch live data from brokers and other apps) to consolidate investment holdings across platforms into one dashboard with daily updates and automatic reminders for SIP dates and tax events.

items.title: Testing Google's Gemini 4 Neon for Billing Error Detection
points: Users can download a year of utility bills as PDFs and bank payment history as CSV, then feed both into a Gemini 4 Neon chat with Thinking level set to High to find billing discrepancies.
The model can generate a month-by-month usage/rate/total table, flag which month jumped and why, and cite exact evidence locations (PDF page, line number, or bank row) for verification.
Recommended workflow: draft a dispute email with verified dates and amounts, and always ask the model to name evidence locations so answers can be spot-checked in about a minute.

items.title: Tech Stock Market Selloff
points: The Nasdaq fell over 5% on Friday, erasing all 2026 gains as three major indexes dropped simultaneously.
Three concurrent pressures drove the decline: concerns that Anthropic's IPO signals a peak in the AI investment cycle, post-election regulatory tightening fears, and elevated inflation data.
Wharton professor Jeremy Siegel characterized the downturn as an overdue correction after three strong years rather than a structural problem.

items.title: Thinking Machines Releases Compact Multimodal Model
points: Thinking Machines released Inkling 2 Mini, a laptop-sized multimodal AI model that can run on a 32GB Mac using a new looped transformer design (a neural network architecture that reuses layers iteratively to save memory).
The release positions the company to compete with China's dominance in open-weight AI models (models whose underlying parameters are publicly released for anyone to run or modify).

items.title: Building Organizational 'Context Systems' for AI
points: Notion co-founder Akshay Kothari published a guide, reaching 6.5M+ views and 24K bookmarks, advocating centralized company knowledge repositories instead of siloed individual AI chatbot conversations.
A 'context system' replaces dozens of individual AI conversations with a shared knowledge base, enabling continuous learning and automation across departments.
Organizations are encouraged to document processes step-by-step across teams so AI agents can handle routine work at scale while employees shift into supervisory roles.
As the shared system grows, AI utility compounds — more context enables better automation and less manual repetition of similar tasks.

items.title: Claude Artifacts for Executive Reporting
points: Claude's Artifacts feature now lets executives auto-generate 60-second KPI recap videos pulling data directly from data warehouses.
